terms.gloss: the climate of a place; its sky and weather
evidence: Liv. 5.54.3: hoc caelum, sub quō nātus ēducātusque essem (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The classical word: the sky over a place, and so its air, weather and climate (Lewis & Short). It takes adjectives freely: caelum salūbre (Cic. Div. 1.130), palustre (Liv. 22.2.11), and gravitās caelī is an unhealthy climate (Cic. Att. 11.22.2). Its first sense is the sky (see sky); for the weather of one day see weather.

evidence: Cic. N.D. 2.13: commoda, quae percipiuntur caelī temperātiōne (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Cicero’s phrase; Tacitus says caelī temperiēs (Ann. 4.67, below). Both mean a climate tempered between heat and cold, not any climate.

terms.gloss: a zone of latitude, a “clime”; in late Latin also climate
evidence: Vitr. 1.1.10 (as a Greek word); Apul., Tert., Mart. Cap. (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The Greek word means a slope, and so a zone of the earth between two parallels of latitude: that is its sense in Vitruvius, who still writes it as Greek. It means a climate only in late writers. Morgan–Owens gives it beside caelum, of a climate zone; in everyday speech caelum is the Latin.

phrases.latin: caelum, nōn animum mūtant, quī trāns mare currunt
phrases.english: those who rush across the sea change their sky, not their mind

phrases.latin: caelī temperiēs hieme mītis objectū montis quō saeva ventōrum arcentur
phrases.english: the climate is mild in winter, for a mountain stands in the way and keeps off the cruel winds

phrases.latin: hoc caelum, sub quō nātus ēducātusque essem
phrases.english: this climate, under which I had been born and brought up

sources: Lewis & Short: caelum · Lewis & Short: temperatio · Lewis & Short: temperies · Lewis & Short: clima
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 135, 292. Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. climate.
